sections.heading: Vehicle Warning Devices
sections.text:
The term ‘Warning Light’ shall refer to:

(a) Any device capable of flashing, steady, rotating, or oscillating an emissive light in amber or amber-and-white colors. This definition shall not include factory-installed vehicle lighting used exclusively for signaling turns, lane changes, hazard lights, or manual headlight flashing.

The term ‘Emergency Light’ shall refer to:

(a) Any device capable of flashing, steady, rotating, or oscillating an emissive light in red, blue, red-and-blue, blue-and white, or red-and-white color combinations. This definition shall not include factory-installed vehicle lighting used exclusively for braking, signaling turns, lane changes, reverse operation, tail illumination, or manual headlight flashing.

The term ‘Siren’ shall refer to:

(a) Any mechanical, electronic, or electro-mechanical device capable of producing a loud, high-pitched oscillating sound, typically intended to signal urgency, assert right-of-way, or alert nearby individuals or vehicles to the presence of an emergency or special-purpose vehicle.

The term ‘Airhorn’ shall refer to:

(a) Any mechanical, electronic, electro-mechanical, or pressure-powered device designed to emit a loud, non-oscillating tone, typically used to provide warning of a vehicle’s approach or to clear traffic. Airhorns are distinct from standard vehicle horns in volume, function, and purpose, and are commonly associated with emergency or special-purpose vehicles.

The term ‘Restricted Signal Light’ shall refer to:

(a) Any device capable of flashing, steady, rotating, or oscillating a green or purple emissive light, whether used alone or in combination with other colors. These lights are typically associated with specialized functions outside of typical emergency or warning lights.

The term ‘Special Equipment’ shall refer to:

(a) Any non-standard equipment affixed to a motor vehicle or equipment that is intended to provide visual or auditory signals for the purpose of asserting presence, indicating authority, ensuring operational safety, or responding to emergencies. This includes, but is not limited to, emergency lights, warning lights, sirens, airhorns, restricted signal lights, beacons, and any similar signaling devices. “Special Equipment” does not include factory-installed lighting or horns intended solely for standard vehicle signaling or manufacturer compliance with traffic safety regulations.

No individual or organization shall operate or cause to be operated any motor vehicle or equipment that displays, shows, or is equipped with emergency lights, unless the vehicle falls under one of the following categories:

(a) Vehicles owned or leased by a government agency and operated by a law enforcement officer, correctional officer, conservation officer, or other individual authorized by statute while acting in the course of their official duties.

(i) Personally owned or civilian vehicles may only be equipped with or display emergency lights for official on-duty use, and only if first approved by the head of the employing agency and the individual holds a valid and active emergency light permit issued by the Division of Motor Vehicles pursuant to 6 M.S.C. 4 § 3401.

(1) However, a personally owned or civilian vehicle operated by a law enforcement officer may be temporarily equipped with emergency lighting issued directly by their employing agency (such as lighting devices distributed through department-authorized equipment lockers/shops) provided such use is strictly limited to official on-duty assignments and the lighting is deactivated, removed, and properly discarded during off-duty periods. This shall not require a separate permit from the Division of Motor Vehicles, so long as the use is authorized by the officer’s employing agency and conducted in accordance with official agency policy and Division of Motor Vehicles regulation.

(b) Vehicles owned or leased by a government agency, or by an organization that is formally contracted or designated by the government of a county or municipality to provide emergency medical or fire protection services, where such government is legally responsible for such services under applicable law, and operated by a firefighter, emergency medical technician, paramedic, or other emergency services personnel while acting in the course of their official duties.

(i) Personally owned or civilian vehicles may only be equipped with or display emergency lights when used for official on-duty purposes, or by county or municipal volunteer firefighters while responding directly to a designated headquarters or response station to report for duty in response to an actual emergency. In either case, such use must be first approved by the head of the employing agency, and the individual must hold a valid and active emergency light permit issued by the Division of Motor Vehicles pursuant to 6 M.S.C. 4 § 3401.

(c) Vehicles owned or operated by an individual or organization that holds a valid and active emergency light permit issued by the Division of Motor Vehicles pursuant to 6 M.S.C. 4 § 3401.

No individual or organization shall operate or cause to be operated any motor vehicle or equipment that displays, shows, or is equipped with warning lights, unless the vehicle falls under one of the following categories:

(a) Vehicles owned or leased by a licensed private patrol operator (PPO), operated by a state-certified private security officer, and clearly marked as a private security vehicle, while actively engaged in the performance of official security duties on private property. A PPO must hold a valid and active warning light permit issued by the Division of Motor Vehicles in order to lawfully equip or display warning lights if the vehicle is unmarked or is not a vehicle explicitly added by the game developers for use by the PPO.

(i) Warning lights on vehicles owned or leased by a licensed private patrol operator may only be displayed on public property when the vehicle is operated by a state-certified security officer, and when such use is essential to the performance of official security duties, or when expressly authorized for temporary use during an active emergency by an on-duty supervisor of a law enforcement agency. Any such use must comply with the provisions of 4 M.S.C. 6 § 1504. Warning lights shall not interfere with the normal flow of public traffic or the operations of emergency services, except where temporary traffic control or road closures have been expressly authorized under 4 M.S.C. 6 § 1504 due to a significant public safety concern. Unauthorized or non-essential use of warning lights on public property is strictly prohibited. All private security officers and their vehicles remain subject to the provisions of the Mayflower Traffic Code (Title 2 of the M.S.C.) at all times.

(b) Vehicles owned or leased by a government agency and operated as road or street maintenance equipment, road service vehicles, mail carrier vehicles, or public transit vehicles, when actively in operation or when a hazard exists.

(c) Vehicles owned or leased by a government agency, when actively engaged in official duties and the use of warning lights is necessary due to hazardous conditions, operational safety, or public visibility, provided such use is permitted by the Division of Motor Vehicles pursuant to 6 M.S.C. 4 § 3401.

(d) Vehicles owned or operated by an individual or organization that holds a valid and active warning light permit issued by the Division of Motor Vehicles pursuant to 6 M.S.C. 4 § 3401.

No individual or organization shall operate or cause to be operated any motor vehicle or equipment that displays, shows, or is equipped with restricted signal lights, unless the vehicle falls under one of the following categories:

(a) Vehicles owned or leased by a government agency, or by an organization formally contracted or designated by a county or municipal government to provide emergency medical or fire protection services, where such government is legally responsible for said services under applicable law, and operated by incident commanders, supervisory personnel, or other authorized public safety officials during active emergency operations, where green restricted signal lights are used exclusively for scene coordination and visibility. Use under this category shall not require a separate Restricted Signal Light Permit if the vehicle is owned and operated by a government agency or contractor described above, and the use is limited to official incident management duties authorized by agency policy.

(b) Vehicles operated by licensed funeral homes or contracted funeral escort services, operated by an authorized employee or agent, when actively leading or managing a funeral procession. Use under this category requires that the individual or organization operating the vehicle holds a valid and active restricted signal light permit issued by the Division of Motor Vehicles pursuant to 6 M.S.C. 4 § 3401.

(i) All purple restricted signal permittees remain subject to the Mayflower Vehicle Code (Title 2 of the M.S.C.) at all times.

(c) Vehicles owned or operated by a government agency, public institution, or licensed organization, and operated by authorized personnel, when used during parades, demonstrations, training, or similar pre-approved special events where green restricted signal lights are necessary for visibility or event coordination. Use under this category requires that the individual or organization operating the vehicle holds a valid and active restricted signal light permit issued by the Division of Motor Vehicles pursuant to 6 M.S.C. 4 § 3401.

(d) Vehicles owned or operated by an individual or organization that holds a valid and active restricted signal light permit issued by the Division of Motor Vehicles pursuant to 6 M.S.C. 4 § 3401.

Vehicles owned by a historical society, museum, or otherwise licensed historical organization may be maintained and operated on public roadways, even if not fully compliant with standard equipment regulations, provided the vehicle and its equipment are at least twenty-five (25) years old from the current date. Such vehicles may not be equipped with or utilize emergency lights, warning lights, sirens, airhorns, or restricted signal lights on public roadways unless expressly permitted by the Division of Motor Vehicles pursuant to 6 M.S.C. 4 § 3401.

No individual or organization shall operate or cause to be operated any motor vehicle or equipment that is equipped with or emits sound through a siren, unless the vehicle falls under one of the following categories:

(a) Vehicles authorized to display emergency lights under 6 M.S.C. 4 § 3202(a) or 6 M.S.C. 4 § 3202(b).

(b) Vehicles owned or operated by an individual or organization that holds a valid and active emergency light permit issued by the Division of Motor Vehicles pursuant to 6 M.S.C. 4 § 3401, and has received separate, express authorization from the Division to equip and utilize a siren. Possession of an emergency light permit alone shall not constitute authorization for siren use.

No individual or organization shall operate or cause to be operated any motor vehicle or equipment that is equipped with or emits sound through an airhorn, unless the vehicle falls under one of the following categories:

(a) Vehicles authorized to use a siren pursuant to 6 M.S.C. 4 § 3301(a) or 6 M.S.C. 4 § 3301(b).

(b) Vehicles authorized to use warning lights pursuant to 6 M.S.C. 4 § 3203(a), provided their use is essential to the performance of official security duties. Use of airhorns by private security shall be limited to active emergencies, hazardous conditions, or similar situations requiring immediate attention.

(c) Vehicles authorized to use warning lights pursuant to 6 M.S.C. 4 § 3203(b) or (c), when engaged in public safety, protective services, or governmental security functions.

(d) Vehicles owned or operated by an individual or organization that holds a valid and active warning light permit or restricted signal light permit issued by the Division of Motor Vehicles pursuant to 6 M.S.C. 4 § 3401, and has received separate, express authorization from the Division to equip and utilize an airhorn. Possession of a warning light permit or restricted signal light permit alone shall not constitute authorization for airhorn use.

The Division of Motor Vehicles shall be authorized, at its discretion, to issue written permits authorizing an individual or organization to equip and utilize vehicles with special equipment, in accordance with the provisions of this Chapter. Such authorization shall permit the use of special equipment on vehicles owned or operated by the permit holder, subject to all applicable laws, Division regulations, and any conditions specified in the permit. The Division may issue such permits upon determining that the proposed use of special equipment is reasonably necessary to ensure the safety of personnel, equipment, or the general public during the performance of official duties or operational functions, or is otherwise deemed necessary by the Division based on unique operational needs or circumstances. Nothing in this section shall obligate the Division to approve any permit application. All permits shall be subject to periodic review and may be modified, suspended, or revoked at the sole discretion of the Division.

The Division shall maintain a current registry of all active permits.

The Division of Motor Vehicles shall have the authority to promulgate rules and regulations necessary to carry out the provisions of this Chapter, including but not limited to defining and clarifying the essential use, operational limits, and display standards of specialized vehicle equipment. Such regulations shall carry the force of law and may be enforced pursuant to 2 M.S.C. §§ 1107 and 1108.

Any individual or organization that operates, or causes to be operated, a motor vehicle equipped with or utilizing special equipment in violation of 6 M.S.C. 4 § 3202, § 3203, § 3301, or § 3302 shall be subject to the penalties established under 2 M.S.C. § 1107. This includes the unauthorized installation, possession, or activation of emergency lights, warning lights, sirens, airhorns, or restricted signal lights without proper legal authority or exemption.

Any individual or organization found to be in violation of a permit condition, regulation, or directive issued by the Division of Motor Vehicles pursuant to this Chapter shall be subject to penalties under 2 M.S.C. § 1108. This includes, but is not limited to, the improper use, abuse, or misrepresentation of special equipment authorized under a DMV-issued permit.

sections.heading: Transportation and Aviation Administration
sections.text:
“Pilot Training Program” or “PTP” shall be defined as: The mandated curriculum enacted by the State Aviation Advisory Board for individuals seeking a pilot certification.

“Pilot-in-Command” or “PIC” shall be defined as: The person who has final authority and responsibility for the operation and safety of the flight; who has been designated as the PIC before or during the flight; and who holds the appropriate category, class, and type rating, if appropriate, for the conduct of the flight.

For the purposes of this subchapter, “Person” shall be defined as: An individual, firm, partnership, corporation, company, association, joint-stock association, or governmental entity. It includes a trustee, receiver, assignee, or similar representative person.

For the purposes of this subchapter, “Aircraft” shall be defined as: A device or machine that is used or intended to be used for flight in the air.

For the purposes of this subchapter, “Airport” shall be defined as: An area of land or water that is used or intended to be used for the landing and takeoff of aircraft, and includes its buildings and facilities, if applicable.

For the purposes of this subchapter, “Practical Test” shall be defined as: A test on the areas of operations for an airman certificate, rating, or authorization is conducted by having the applicant respond to questions and demonstrate maneuvers in flight, in a flight simulator, or a flight training device.

For the purposes of this subchapter, “Heliport” shall be defined as: An area of land, water, or structure used or intended to be used for the landing and takeoff of helicopters.

The Mayflower Department of Transportation shall be established (hereinafter “Mayflower Department of Transportation”, “Department of Transportation”, “department”, or “MDOT”).

(a) For the purposes of Article V, Section II of the State Constitution, the Mayflower Department of Transportation shall be considered a principal department.

The head of the Department of Transportation shall be the Secretary of Transportation, who shall be appointed by the Governor, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate.

The department shall be composed of the Secretary of Transportation, the Deputy Secretary of Transportation, and a reasonable amount of support staff.

The Mayflower Aviation Administration (hereinafter “Mayflower Aviation Administration, “Aviation Administration”, “Administration”, or “MAA”) shall be established as a subordinate agency of the Mayflower Department of Transportation.

The Secretary of Transportation shall have direct supervision of the administration and appoint an Administrator, who shall serve at the pleasure of the Secretary of Transportation and shall be responsible for the direction and management of the administration.

The Administrator of the Aviation Administration shall:

(a) Be the final authority for carrying out all functions, powers, and duties of the Administration relating to: the appointment and employment of all officers and employees of the Administration (other than gubernatorial and political appointees); the acquisition and maintenance of property, services, and equipment of the Administration; the promulgation of regulations, rules, orders, circulars, bulletins, and other official publications of the Administration, except as otherwise provided; and any other obligation imposed on or power conferred upon the Administrator.

An individual not holding one of the certificates or licenses outlined in this section may not operate or serve as the pilot in command of an aircraft. (c) Maintenance, operation, and inspection of aircraft;

parts.heading: Subchapter VI — REGULATORY POWERS AND ENFORCEMENT

sections.heading: Flight Safety and Restrictions
sections.text:
For the purposes of this chapter, “Aircraft” shall be defined as:

(a) A device or machine that is used or intended to be used for flight in the air.

For the purposes of this chapter, “Civilian Pilot-in-Command” shall be defined as:

(a) The person who has final authority and responsibility for the operation and safety of a privately owned Aircraft.

For the purposes of this chapter, “State Pilot-in-Command” shall be defined as:

(a) The person, who is an on-duty guardsman or government employee, who is authorised to operate an aircraft and who has final authority and responsibility for the operation and safety of a government owned Aircraft.

For the purposes of this chapter, “Airport” shall be defined as:

(a) An area of land or water that is used or intended to be used for the landing and takeoff of aircraft, and includes its buildings and facilities, if applicable; this definition shall not refer to or include heliports.

For the purposes of this chapter, “Heliport” shall be defined as:

(a) An area of land, water, or structure that is used or intended to be used for the landing and takeoff of helicopters, and includes its buildings and facilities, if applicable.

All Airports shall be considered a Firearm Free Zone.

In any Airport, it shall be illegal to be in possession of—

(a) An item capable of causing harm; or

(b) A facial concealment device.

Law enforcement officers or other security personnel designated by the Secretary of Transportation may search any person who is seeking access to an airport or is within an airport.

Law enforcement officers or other security personnel designated by the Secretary of Transportation may exercise lethal force against any person who is inside or within 50 studs of an airport and possesses an explosive device.

The Mayflower Aviation Administration shall maintain a public database which outlines any property which an aircraft may not fly over.

The Mayflower Aviation Administration may promulgate rules and regulations which dictate—

(a) A minimum altitude requirement for a Civilian Pilot-in-Command when operating an Aircraft;

(b) Areas of the state where an Aircraft may not fly over; and

(c) Areas of the state where an Aircraft may not be within a certain amount of studs of.

It shall be required by law that a Civilian Pilot-in-Command may not operate an Aircraft in the airspace above—

(a) The Capitol Building;

(b) Prison complexes; and

(c) Military Exclusion Zones.

Military or law enforcement personnel shall be authorized to shoot down unauthorized aircraft in restricted airspace by a Senior Officer of the National Guard or a member of the National Guard’s Aviation Unit.

Air Traffic Controllers shall direct pilots and aircraft to avoid protective zones as designated by 3 M.S.C. 1 § 1501, if an aircraft fails to heed warnings of ATC and continues to operate within a protective zone, law enforcement or military personnel establishing the protective zone shall be authorized to shoot down the aircraft.

State Pilot-in-Commands may request exemptions from Flight Codes and No Fly Zones from the Mayflower Aviation Administration.

(a) Government agencies which employ State Pilot-in-Commands may request exemptions on behalf of their State-Pilot-in-Commands.

(b) Approved No Fly Zones exemptions may be referred to as “Temporary Flight Restrictions” and must be publicly accessible through a discord channel.

Any individual who is in possession of an item capable of doing harm or a facial concealment device within an Airport or Heliport shall be liable for arrest for 1 M.S.C. § 3205 "Trespassing."

Any individual who refuses to be searched within an Airport and remains within an Airport shall be liable for arrest for 1 M.S.C. § 3205 “Trespassing."

Any individual who refuses to be searched within a Heliport and remains within a Heliport shall be liable for arrest for 1 M.S.C. § 3205 "Trespassing."

All heliports shall be considered a Firearm Free Zone.

In any heliport, it shall be illegal to—

(a) Possess an item capable of causing harm; or

(b) If not an on-duty law enforcement officer or guardsman, possess or wear a facial concealment device (mask).

Law enforcement officers or other security personnel designated by the Secretary of Transportation may search any person who is seeking access to a heliport or is within a heliport.

Law enforcement officers or other security personnel designated by the Secretary of Transportation may exercise lethal force against any person who is inside or within 50 studs of a heliport and possesses an explosive device.

DEFINITIONS. “Tail Number” shall be defined as the combination of letters and numbers assigned to a specific civilian aircraft displayed on the upper sides of a civilian aircraft.

For the purposes of this act, “Registry” or “Registries” shall refer to any database, registry, list, document, or collection containing tail numbers of civilian aircraft.

REGISTRY PROHIBITIONS. Notwithstanding 6 M.S.C. 6 § 1401 and 6 M.S.C. 6 § 1601, the Mayflower Aviation Administration may not create any regulation, rule, directive, mandate, order, announcement, or policy forcing owners of civilian aircraft to submit their tail numbers to a registry.

The Mayflower Aviation Administration may not create any registry containing tail numbers of civilian aircraft.

(a) The Mayflower Aviation Administration shall destroy and erase all registries containing tail numbers of civilian aircraft.

(b) The Aircraft Identification Registry and all of its related documents shall be destroyed and deleted.

The Mayflower Aviation Administration may not force any pilot to leak the tail number associated with any civilian aircraft.

(a) All pilots shall enjoy the right of keeping their tail numbers private.

(b) All pilots shall enjoy the right of not having their tail number noted down on any registry.

If the Mayflower Aviation Administration is found violating any contents of this act, the Department of Justice shall investigate the Mayflower Aviation Administration for any findings of registries containing tail numbers of civilian aircraft.

sections.heading: Fishing and Wildlife Management
sections.text:
The term "conservation officer" shall refer to:

(a) Any person employed by the Mayflower Parks and Wildlife Department for the purposes of enforcing this Title.

(b) Any person considered a peace officer under the Police Services and Community Safety Act.

The term "fish" includes:

(a) parts of fish;

(b) shellfish, crustaceans, marine animals and any parts of shellfish, crustaceans or marine animals; and

(c) the eggs, sperm, spawn, larvae, spat and juvenile stages of fish, shellfish, crustaceans and marine animals.

The term "fishing license" shall refer to:

(a) A license or permit issued under this Title for the purposes of capturing fish, but does not include a commercial license.

The term "commercial fishing license" shall refer to:

(a) A license or permit issued under this Title to a registered business entity.

The term "Director of Parks and Wildlife" shall refer to:

(a) The Director of the Mayflower Parks and Wildlife Department.

The term "fish habitat" shall refer to:

(a) Water frequented by fish and any other areas on which fish depend directly or indirectly to carry out their life processes.

The term "capture device" shall refer to:

(a) Any machine, equipment, or contrivance specifically designed for and capable of capturing, retrieving, or securing fish.

The term "fishing area" shall refer to:

(a) Land within 50 studs of any lake, river, or stream—in addition to the body of water itself—within the state that does not fall on private property, in addition to any bridge, port, pier or dock that is publicly accessible

The term "area of cultural significance or natural beauty" shall refer to:

(a) Any site that is designated through resolution by the State Senate to be of cultural significance to the people of the State or the Union and those of significant natural beauty.

The term "protected forest" shall refer to:

(a) Any area designated by the State Senate through resolution in which logging is prohibited.

Any person who wishes to capture fish in any fish habitat shall be required to possess a fishing license.

Any registered business which, as a part of its business operations, captures fish in a fish habitat shall be required to possess a commercial fishing license.

(a) Upon receiving a commercial fishing license, the owner of the business entity or the employee in charge of obtaining the commercial fishing license shall notify the Department of State of such.

(b) Any employee of a business entity with a commercial fishing license does not exempt them from the requirement to possess a fishing license as stipulated in 7 M.S.C. 1 § 1201.

Any person may possess a capture device, however no person shall use a capture device to capture fish in any fish habitat unless:

(a) that person possesses a fishing license; or

Any person observed by a conservation officer to be engaged in capturing fish, with or without the use of a capture device, shall be required to display their fishing license.

(a) Any person that is an employee of a business entity that possesses a commercial fishing license and is engaged in capturing fish for that business entity must, in addition to this code, communicate to the conservation officer the business entity that they are working under.

Any person in possession of a fishing license and is observed by a conservation officer to be engaged in capturing fish shall have their person liable and current vehicle to search by the aforementioned conservation officer provided that there are reasonable grounds to do so.

(a) Any person upon purchasing or obtaining a fishing license agrees that if they are observed to be engaged in capturing fish by a conservation officer, with or without the use of a capture device, then their person and current vehicle is liable to search by the aforementioned conservation officer provided that there are reasonable grounds to do so.

(b) An observation of a person engaged in capturing fish is considered void if the conservation officer loses direct line of sight to the person at any point in time.

Any person who obtains, whether by fishing or by not fishing, any fish stipulated in 7 M.S.C. 2 § 3101 shall dispose of the fish by removing it from their immediate person or external method of storage.

If an employee of the Mayflower Parks and Wildlife Department is not considered a peace officer under 7 M.S.C. 1 § 1101 but is still considered a conservation officer under 7 M.S.C. 1 § 1101, then they may issue citations for offenses listed in Subtitle 2 of this Title in accordance with department guidelines.

Conservation officers shall be limited to enforcing Title 7 and shall not act as peace officers unless officially designated and registered as such by the Director of Parks and Wildlife.

(a) This does not prevent them from acting in defense of self/others or ensuring the safety of the public in absence of law enforcement.

Any Parks and Wildlife tactical or investigations unit/body must be composed solely of certified peace officers and is also bound by the provisions of this act.

Members of the Parks and Wildlife Department shall have the ability to enact road closure within a state park for the purpose of—

(a) responding to and clearing motor vehicle accidents;

(b) clearing and or otherwise managing hazards on roadways within a state park;

(c) enforcing Title 7; or

(d) conducting maintenance on a public road within a state park.

Provided at least one Parks and Wildlife peace officer is present, members of the Parks and Wildlife Department shall have the ability to conduct checkpoints within a state park for the purpose of:

(a) enforcing Title 7 and conducting Title 7 inspections.

(i) Any person traveling within a state park may be subject to a Title 7 inspection at an established checkpoint within a state park.

Parks and Wildlife peace officers shall enforce and/or investigate elements of the criminal code (Title 1 of the M.S.C.) and elements of the vehicle code (Title 2 of the M.S.C), subject to the limitation that at least one of the following criteria must be met:

(a) The offender endangers or harms Parks and Wildlife Department personnel; visitors utilizing Parks and Wildlife facilities; players engaging in recreational or natural resource (including but not limited to fishing, logging, hunting, and mining) activities;

(b) The offense was committed against or in relation to the Parks and Wildlife Department;

(c) The offense was committed within or in eyesight of any of the following: property or infrastructure owned, maintained, or administered by the Parks and Wildlife Department; official operations or events conducted by the Parks and Wildlife Department; designated natural resource (including but not limited to fishing, logging, hunting, and mining) or recreational areas; state or local parks, hiking trails, and camping grounds;

(d) The offense relates to environmental harm or illegal natural resource activities;

(e) A Parks and Wildlife peace officer witnesses a felony offense or an offense that poses a significant danger to the general public or a threat to public safety;

(f) A Parks and Wildlife peace officer is participating in an inter-agency task force or any other similar assignment; or

(g) A State of Emergency is declared.

Parks and Wildlife peace officers shall enforce and/or investigate elements of conservation law (Title 7 of Mayflower State Code) anywhere within the state.

(a) Parks and Wildlife peace officers shall be empowered to conduct traffic stops on players seen or known to be engaged in activities defined under Title 7. These traffic stops shall be known as “Title 7 traffic stops”.

(b) The primary purpose of Title 7 traffic stops shall be to conduct Title 7 inspections. However, it shall be permitted for Parks and Wildlife peace officers to ensure that: the driver of the vehicle they stopped has an active driver’s license; the driver of the vehicle has no warrants; and the vehicle is not stolen. If other criminal code or vehicle code violations are observed while conducting a Title 7 traffic stop, Parks and Wildlife peace officers may take appropriate law enforcement action.

Parks and Wildlife peace officers may: overall ensure public safety within the scope of their duties; support the Parks and Wildlife Department; and collaborate with other law enforcement officers and public safety officials to support their duties.

(a) Parks and Wildlife peace officers may assist other peace officers who request assistance. This includes but is not limited to “10-58”, “58” (or its equivalent, e.g. panic buttons) calls on the radio or when Parks and Wildlife peace officer assistance is specifically requested.

(b) Parks and Wildlife peace officers shall have the authority to engage in pursuits only if an offender flees from Parks and Wildlife peace officers and/or conservation officers who are actively or attempting to detain or arrest an individual, given the aforementioned criteria for enforcing the criminal or vehicle code are met, or if assisting other peace officers as per this Act.

Parks and Wildlife peace officers may perform any other reasonable duties or functions at the discretion of the Director of the Parks and Wildlife Department.

Violations of this subchapter shall be corrected by the Parks and Wildlife internal affairs body.

(a) Water frequented by fish and any other areas on which fish depend directly or indirectly to carry out their life processes.

(a) Any area designated by the State Senate through resolution in which logging is prohibited.

sections.text:

sections.heading: Protected Species and Resources
sections.text:
Any of the following fish shall be considered prohibited for the purposes of 7 M.S.C. 2 § 1102:

(a) Protected fish shall include:

(i) Trollfish, provided that the trollfish is of the twenty (20), twenty-four (24), or thirty (30) pound variant.

(ii) Minishark, provided that the minishark is of the forty (40), fifty (50), or sixty (60) pound variant.

(b) Undersized fish shall include:

(i) Salmon, provided that the salmon is of the eight (8) pound variant.

(ii) Trout, provided that the trout is of the twelve (12) pound variant.

(iii) Clam, provided that the clam is of the one (1) pound variant.

(c) Oversized fish shall include:

(i) Bass, provided that the bass is of the sixteen (16) pound variant.

(ii) Lobster, provided that the lobster is of the four (4) pound variant.

(iii) Sturgeon, provided that the sturgeon is of the fifty (50) pound variant.

Any of the following trees shall be prohibited for the purposes of 7 M.S.C. 2 § 1202.

(a) Protected trees shall include:

(i) Amaranth Trees.

(ii) Rosewood Trees.

sections.text: The Mayflower Parks and Wildlife Department shall have the jurisdiction to conduct their lawful duties which shall include the enforcement of Title 7, the operation of established local/state parks, protected forests and designated areas of cultural significance or natural beauty, and any other additional duties established within the Mayflower State Code.
